Patiently
pā'shent-lĭ
adv. (with patience; enduring without murmuring; waiting without fretting)
Latin patiens, suffering, bearing, from pati, to suffer. Patience in Scripture is not placidity of temperament but endurance under a weight.

Biblical Definition

David's two great patience texts sit in adjacent psalms and give the two halves of the grace. Psalm 37: “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass” (Psa 37:7) — patience defined against a specific irritant, the visible success of a wicked man. Psalm 40 gives the outcome: “I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry” (Psa 40:1), and what follows is the horrible pit, the miry clay, the rock, the new song. Paul asks Agrippa to hear him patiently (Act 26:3), the courtesy of a prisoner who has one hearing and needs it not to be cut short. And Hebrews gives the pattern case: “after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise” (Heb 6:15) — Abraham, twenty-five years between the promise of a son and Isaac's birth, and the whole argument of the passage is that God swore by Himself because He could swear by no greater, so that we might have strong consolation. Patience in Scripture is therefore never passive resignation. It is active waiting on a God who has bound Himself by an oath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines patiently as with calmness or composure; without discontent or murmuring; without repining; with the temper that endures evils.

expand to see more

PATIENTLY, adv. With calmness or composure; without discontent or murmuring.

2. Without vexation or discontent; without haste.

PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.

Key Scripture

Psa 37:7 — "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass."

Psa 40:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry."

Heb 6:15 — "And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 37 is the answer to a question the age asks constantly — why the wicked prosper — and it answers not with an explanation but with a command not to fret and a horizon of judgment.

expand to see more

Psalm 37 opens by naming the exact temptation: fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. It repeats the command three times in the first eight verses, and it never once explains why God permits their prosperity. Instead it changes the time horizon: for they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb. Asaph works the same problem in Psalm 73 and describes the collapse it nearly caused in him — my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped — and the turn comes not from an argument but from a place: until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. Our age poses the prosperity of the wicked as a philosophical objection to God's existence, and Christians frequently try to answer it as though it were one. Scripture treats it as a temptation to envy, and prescribes accordingly: rest, wait, fret not, delight thyself also in the LORD, commit thy way unto him. The patience commanded is not an agreement to stop caring about injustice — the same psalm promises that the meek shall inherit the earth and that the LORD laughs at the wicked, for he seeth that his day is coming. It is a refusal to settle accounts on a timescale shorter than God's. Abraham waited twenty-five years and obtained the promise; the psalmist waited and got a rock under his feet and a new song in his mouth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chuwl (H2342), to wait, to writhe in waiting; qavah (H6960), to wait, to look eagerly for; Greek makrothumeo (G3114), to be long-tempered, to endure patiently.

expand to see more

Hebrew chuwl (H2342) — to wait, and also to writhe or travail; the waiting of Psalm 37:7 is not comfortable; Psalm 37:7.

Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; Psalm 40:1, Isaiah 40:31.

Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be long-tempered, to bear long; Abraham patiently enduring, and the husbandman waiting for the precious fruit of the earth; Hebrews 6:15, James 5:7.

Usage

"“Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself” — patience defined against a specific irritant."

"“I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me” — and a new song followed."

"“After he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise” — twenty-five years, and an oath behind it."
